match.reason: No point in the bank teaches how a rising or falling exchange rate changes import and export prices and inflation; e-govtrade only mentions a weaker currency in passing as one influence on net trade, which is a related but narrower idea.

draft.title: Appreciation and depreciation
card: a rise in the value of the Australian dollar against another currency. For example, A$1 buys US$0.70 instead of US$0.65.
a fall in the value of the Australian dollar against another currency. For example, A$1 buys US$0.60 instead of US$0.65.
When the dollar appreciates, imports become cheaper in Australian dollars. Australian exports become dearer for overseas buyers, so exporters may find it harder to compete.
When the dollar depreciates, exports become cheaper for overseas buyers, which helps exporters. Imports cost more in Australian dollars, which can add to inflation, a general rise in prices.
draft.remember: A higher dollar favours importers and buyers of imports. A lower dollar favours exporters but can push prices up.

a.q: The Australian dollar appreciates against the euro. What is the most likely effect on a shop that imports Italian furniture?
opts: Its furniture costs less in Australian dollars
Its furniture costs more in Australian dollars
Its furniture price stays the same in euros and dollars
Its furniture becomes dearer for Italian buyers
a.why: A stronger dollar buys more euros, so goods priced in euros cost fewer Australian dollars. Option two reverses the effect, which would happen if the dollar depreciated.
a.clue: A stronger dollar buys more foreign money.

b.q: Jess grows wine grapes in Mildura and sells wine to Canada. The Australian dollar depreciates against the Canadian dollar. What is the most likely effect?
opts: Her wine becomes cheaper for Canadian buyers
Her wine becomes dearer for Canadian buyers
Her costs for imported machinery fall
Inflation in Australia is likely to fall
b.why: A lower Australian dollar means Canadians need fewer of their dollars to buy her wine, so it is cheaper for them. A common mistake is to think a falling dollar makes imports cheaper, but it raises their price in Australian dollars and can add to inflation.
b.clue: Think about what Canadian buyers must pay in their own currency.

a.best: Its furniture costs less in Australian dollars

b.best: Her wine becomes cheaper for Canadian buyers
